title: Resolving Token-Space Gradient Conflicts: Token Space Manipulation for Transformer-Based Multi-Task Learning
problem_statement: Multi-task learning with pre-trained vision transformers encounters negative transfer when conflicting gradients emerge across different task objectives. Previous dynamic architectures address gradient conflicts by directly converting shared transformer parameters into task-specific parameters, but that strategy incurs severe parameter inefficiency, excessive computational overhead, and high risk of overfitting. Furthermore, existing transformer multi-task architectures rely on rigid module designs with fixed capacity, preventing dynamic allocation of shared and task-specific representations across different network depths.
domain: Multi-task dense computer vision prediction across indoor scene understanding, geometric surface parsing, and semantic segmentation benchmarks (NYUD-v2, PASCAL-Context, and Taskonomy).
theoretical_framework: The authors analyze token representations through Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on the uncentered covariance matrix of shared transformer tokens, partitioning the token space into an orthogonal range space (representing capabilities acquired during pre-training) and a null space (representing unspanned feature directions). Task-specific token gradients are projected onto both subspaces using orthogonal projection operators. Propositions 1 and 2 prove that applying channel-wise affine token modulators in the range space and introducing learnable task-specific tokens in the null space reduce gradient conflicts and alleviate multi-task loss increases.
methodology: The Dynamic Token Modulation and Expansion for Multi-Task Learning (DTME-MTL) framework detects and resolves gradient conflicts within the token space of transformer architectures. Early in the training process, the framework computes the uncentered covariance of shared tokens and applies SVD to separate the range and null spaces using a variance ratio threshold r. When task gradients conflict in the range space, the framework inserts channel-wise affine token modulators (W ⊙ T + b) to rotate and scale shared tokens. When task gradients conflict in the null space, the framework inserts learnable task-specific tokens concatenated with shared tokens before transformer self-attention blocks. These adaptations are selectively applied to the top 25% to 50% most conflicted layers, and the complete network is fine-tuned without freezing the backbone.
datasets: NYUD-v2 — Indoor RGB-D dataset evaluating 4 dense prediction tasks: depth estimation, semantic segmentation, surface normal prediction, and edge detection.

PASCAL-Context — In-the-wild scene understanding dataset evaluating 5 dense prediction tasks: semantic segmentation, human parts estimation, saliency estimation, surface normal prediction, and edge detection.

Taskonomy — Large-scale indoor scene dataset evaluating 11 dense prediction tasks: Depth Euclidean, Depth Zbuffer, Edge Texture, Keypoints 2D, Keypoints 3D, Surface Normal, Principal Curvature, Reshading, Segment Unsupervised 2D, and Segment Unsupervised 2.5D.
ImageNet-22K — Large-scale image classification dataset utilized for pre-training the Vision Transformer backbone encoders (ViT-T, ViT-S, ViT-B, ViT-L).

metrics: Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) for semantic segmentation, human parts estimation, and saliency estimation
Mean angular distance (degrees) between predicted and ground-truth normal vectors for surface normal prediction
Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) for depth estimation and principal curvature
L1 distance for remaining Taskonomy dense prediction tasks
Average multi-task relative performance metric (Δm %) measuring per-task gain or drop relative to single-task baselines
Computational execution time (minutes) for SVD and conflict computation, and inference latency overhead percentage
baselines: Baseline (ST) — Single-task learning upper baseline with dedicated models per task
Baseline (MT) — Multi-task baseline with shared ViT backbone and 3×3 Conv-BN-ReLU task-specific decoders
Dynamic architecture baseline — Recon (layer-wise parameter-level conflict resolution)
Multi-task optimization methods — Gradient Descent (GD), GradDrop, MGDA, PCGrad, CAGrad, IMTL, Nash-MTL, Aligned-MTL, Uncertainty Weighting (UW), Dynamic Weight Average (DWA), and FAMO
State-of-the-art transformer MTL architectures — InvPT and TaskPrompter
architectures: Vision Transformer (ViT) backbones: ViT-Tiny (ViT-T), ViT-Small (ViT-S), ViT-Base (ViT-B), and ViT-Large (ViT-L) pre-trained on ImageNet-22K
Task-specific decoders: single-layer 3×3 Conv-BN-ReLU prediction heads
Multi-task prompting architectures: InvPT and TaskPrompter integrated with DTME-MTL modules

key_findings: DTME-MTL consistently outperforms the multi-task baseline across NYUD-v2 and PASCAL-Context benchmarks while requiring only a 0.2% to 0.3% parameter increase, achieving performance comparable to single-task models without complex architectural modules.

On the 11-task Taskonomy benchmark using ViT-B, DTME-MTL achieves the highest average multi-task improvement of 4.67% with only a 0.118% parameter increase, outperforming previous multi-task optimization methods including CAGrad, Nash-MTL, FAMO, and PCGrad.

DTME-MTL integrates directly with state-of-the-art transformer MTL architectures, improving InvPT and TaskPrompter performance on NYUD-v2 and PASCAL-Context with minimal parameter additions of 0.048% and 0.046% respectively.

Token Modulation (TM) and Token Expansion (TE) resolve distinct conflict mechanisms: TM resolves range-space conflicts while TE resolves null-space conflicts, and swapping the assignment of TM and TE across conflict spaces causes substantial performance degradation.

Selecting layers based on gradient conflict severity outperforms random layer selection and reverse-order selection, with expanding 25% to 50% of the most conflicted layers yielding optimal performance gains.
Overexpansion beyond 50% of transformer layers degrades performance because adding task-specific tokens and modulators to low-conflict layers induces overfitting.
Performing SVD early during training produces better task performance than late-stage expansion because early expansion leverages the pre-trained feature structure.

Training the expanded network without freezing the pre-trained backbone parameters significantly outperforms training with frozen backbones, enabling the model to dynamically partition the token space.

Resolving gradient conflicts in token space avoids the severe overfitting observed in parameter-level expansion methods such as Recon, while enabling parallel multi-task inference with only a 13.4% latency overhead on ViT-B compared to the linear latency scaling of LoRA.
scope_and_delimitations: The empirical evaluation is focused on dense visual prediction tasks on NYUD-v2, PASCAL-Context, and Taskonomy benchmarks using pre-trained Vision Transformer backbones (ViT-T, ViT-S, ViT-B, ViT-L).
The number of task-specific expanded tokens is statically set to six learnable tokens per layer rather than being dynamically adapted per task or per input sample.
The SVD computation and gradient conflict analysis are executed once at an early training stage rather than being recomputed iteratively at every optimization step.
Token modulation and expansion are selectively restricted to the top 25% to 50% most conflicted transformer layers rather than applied across all transformer layers.
The study focuses on transfer learning from pre-trained backbones and does not evaluate training vision transformers from random initialization.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: Performance improves as more high-conflict layers are expanded, but begins to degrade when expansion exceeds 50%, especially when low-conflict layers are included. This suggests that overexpansion can be detrimental. Table [2](#page-6-1) further confirms that using a moderate expansion ratio (50%) avoids overfitting, whereas Fig. [6](#page-13-0) highlights that indiscriminate expansion into less conflicting layers harms performance. These findings underscore the importance of both the *extent* and *location* of TM+TE application.
limitations.summary: The authors acknowledge that expanding beyond 50% of transformer layers degrades multi-task performance because indiscriminate expansion into low-conflict layers causes overfitting. In addition, the method relies on statically allocating a fixed number of six task tokens per layer and requires manual selection of the layer expansion ratio rather than dynamic per-step adaptation.

generalizability_gap: The authors do not evaluate the framework on natural language processing benchmarks, code-switched language understanding, speech processing, reinforcement learning, or multi-modal vision-language foundation models. Furthermore, the experiments examine up to 11 visual tasks, leaving performance on massive multi-task setups with dozens or hundreds of tasks unverified.
methodological_gap: The framework relies on static allocation of six task-specific tokens per layer and computes SVD only once early in training, rather than dynamically adjusting the token count or updating token subspaces iteratively. Additionally, selecting the optimal expansion ratio and activation threshold requires empirical tuning, and the framework lacks an automated routing mechanism to allocate token capacity dynamically during optimization.
